claim: Malaria is responsible for over 600,000 deaths every year, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Malaria remains the deadliest parasitic disease worldwide and is responsible every year for over 600,000 deaths, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa (WHO, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2023 report

claim: Plasmodium sporozoites are inoculated into the skin during the bite of an infected mosquito.
source: Plasmodium sporozoites are inoculated into the skin during the bite of an infected mosquito.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript

claim: The infection caused by Plasmodium parasites begins with the inoculation of the sporozoite stage into the skin by an infected mosquito.
source: The infection, caused by parasites of the genus Plasmodium, begins with the inoculation of the sporozoite stage into the skin by an infected mosquito (Sidjanski and Vanderberg, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sidjanski and Vanderberg, 1997

claim: Sporozoites become activated within the skin and move through the dermis until some find and invade a blood vessel.
source: Within the skin, sporozoites become activated and move through the dermis until some find and invade a blood vessel (Amino et al., 2006; Vanderberg and Frevert, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amino et al., 2006 and Vanderberg and Frevert, 2004

claim: Upon entering circulation, parasites arrest in the liver.
source: Upon entering circulation, parasites arrest in the liver (Tavares et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tavares et al., 2017

claim: Sporozoites cross the sinusoidal barrier within 2–3 hr after entering the liver.
source: cross the sinusoidal barrier within 2–3 hr (Tavares et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tavares et al., 2013

claim: Intracellular parasites replicate massively before being released back into the blood to infect erythrocytes and cause the disease.
source: Intracellular parasites replicate massively before being released back into the blood to infect erythrocytes and cause the disease (Sturm et al., 2006; Tarun et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sturm et al., 2006 and Tarun et al., 2006

claim: The sporozoite surface is covered by a dense coat of the circumsporozoite protein (CSP).
source: The sporozoite surface is covered by a dense coat of the circumsporozoite protein (CSP)
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: CSP has been shown to be an immunodominant protective antigen in a rodent malaria model.
source: The sporozoite surface is covered by a dense coat of the circumsporozoite protein (CSP), shown to be an immunodominant protective antigen in a rodent malaria model (Zavala et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zavala et al., 1983

claim: CSP has a highly conserved structural organization across diverse Plasmodium species, comprising conserved N- and C-terminal domains and a highly variable and repetitive central region.
source: This protein has a highly conserved structural organization across diverse Plasmodium species, comprising conserved N- and C-terminal domains and a highly variable and repetitive central region.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix M are the only two malaria vaccines recommended by the World Health Organization.
source: For example, RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix M, the only two malaria vaccines recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO)
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and WHO recommendations

claim: RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix M vaccines include a fragment of the central repetitive region and the C-terminal domain of the CSP from Plasmodium falciparum.
source: For example, RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix M, the only two malaria vaccines recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), include a fragment of the central repetitive region and the C-terminal domain of the CSP from Plasmodium falciparum (Pf), the most lethal human-infecting parasite (de Almeida et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Almeida et al., 2021

claim: There is a positive correlation between high levels of anti-CSP antibodies induced by the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine and efficacy against malaria.
source: Extensive research has demonstrated a positive correlation between high levels of anti-CSP antibodies (Abs) induced by the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine and efficacy against malaria (White et al., 2013; White et al., 2014; White et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 2013, 2014, and 2015

claim: Anti-CSP monoclonal antibodies protect in vivo against sporozoite infection in mice.
source: Remarkably, anti-CSP monoclonal Abs (mAbs) protect in vivo against sporozoite infection in various experimental settings, including mice (Imkeller et al., 2018; Kisalu et al., 2018; Murugan et al., 2018; Oyen et al., 2017; Potocnjak et al., 1980; Tan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 1980)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies in mice

claim: Anti-CSP monoclonal antibodies protect in vivo against sporozoite infection in monkeys.
source: Remarkably, anti-CSP monoclonal Abs (mAbs) protect in vivo against sporozoite infection in various experimental settings, including mice (Imkeller et al., 2018; Kisalu et al., 2018; Murugan et al., 2018; Oyen et al., 2017; Potocnjak et al., 1980; Tan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 1980), monkeys (Cochrane et al., 1982)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cochrane et al., 1982

claim: Anti-CSP monoclonal antibodies protect in vivo against sporozoite infection in humans.
source: Remarkably, anti-CSP monoclonal Abs (mAbs) protect in vivo against sporozoite infection in various experimental settings, including mice (Imkeller et al., 2018; Kisalu et al., 2018; Murugan et al., 2018; Oyen et al., 2017; Potocnjak et al., 1980; Tan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 1980), monkeys (Cochrane et al., 1982), and humans (Gaudinski et al., 2021; Kayentao et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaudinski et al., 2021; Kayentao et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022

claim: Antibodies that target the CSP central repetitive region exhibit a cytotoxic effect on the sporozoites, accompanied by the shedding of the CSP surface coat.
source: It has been observed that Abs that target the CSP central repetitive region exhibit a cytotoxic effect on the sporozoites, accompanied by the shedding of the CSP surface coat (Stewart and Vanderberg, 1991; Yoshida et al., 1980)
evidence: Supported by citations to Stewart and Vanderberg, 1991 and Yoshida et al., 1980

claim: Anti-CSP antibodies targeting the central repetitive region inhibit sporozoite motility.
source: It has been observed that Abs that target the CSP central repetitive region exhibit a cytotoxic effect on the sporozoites, accompanied by the shedding of the CSP surface coat (Stewart and Vanderberg, 1991; Yoshida et al., 1980), inhibition of motility, loss of infectivity (Hollingdale et al., 1982; Stewart et al., 1986)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hollingdale et al., 1982 and Stewart et al., 1986

claim: Anti-CSP antibodies targeting the central repetitive region cause loss of sporozoite infectivity.
source: It has been observed that Abs that target the CSP central repetitive region exhibit a cytotoxic effect on the sporozoites, accompanied by the shedding of the CSP surface coat (Stewart and Vanderberg, 1991; Yoshida et al., 1980), inhibition of motility, loss of infectivity (Hollingdale et al., 1982; Stewart et al., 1986)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hollingdale et al., 1982 and Stewart et al., 1986

claim: Anti-CSP antibodies targeting the central repetitive region cause parasite death.
source: It has been observed that Abs that target the CSP central repetitive region exhibit a cytotoxic effect on the sporozoites, accompanied by the shedding of the CSP surface coat (Stewart and Vanderberg, 1991; Yoshida et al., 1980), inhibition of motility, loss of infectivity (Hollingdale et al., 1982; Stewart et al., 1986), and parasite death (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023 and Aliprandini et al., 2018

claim: The cytotoxic effects of anti-CSP antibodies are independent of downstream host immune effectors such as the complement and immune host cells.
source: These effects are independent of downstream host immune effectors such as the complement and immune host cells (Aliprandini et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aliprandini et al., 2018

claim: Antibody cytotoxicity increases when parasites are moving in 3D substrates such as the matrix of the cutaneous environment.
source: Instead, Ab cytotoxicity increases when parasites are moving in 3D substrates such as the matrix of the cutaneous environment (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023

claim: Neutralization of sporozoites by anti-CSP antibodies occurs primarily during their migration through the skin.
source: Accordingly, neutralization of sporozoites by anti-CSP Abs occurs primarily during their migration through the skin (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023 and Aliprandini et al., 2018

claim: Neutralization of sporozoites by anti-CSP antibodies in the skin is dependent on sporozoite motility and host cell-wounding activities.
source: Accordingly, neutralization of sporozoites by anti-CSP Abs occurs primarily during their migration through the skin (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018) and is dependent on sporozoite motility and host cell-wounding activities (Aliprandini et al., 2018), which are both crucial for parasite progression in the dermis (Amino et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aliprandini et al., 2018 and Amino et al., 2008

claim: Sporozoite motility and host cell-wounding activities are crucial for parasite progression in the dermis.
source: Accordingly, neutralization of sporozoites by anti-CSP Abs occurs primarily during their migration through the skin (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018) and is dependent on sporozoite motility and host cell-wounding activities (Aliprandini et al., 2018), which are both crucial for parasite progression in the dermis (Amino et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amino et al., 2008

claim: Potent antibodies or high concentrations of them efficiently target sporozoites in the blood and liver following intravenous parasite inoculation which bypasses the skin.
source: Potent Abs or high concentrations of them were shown to efficiently target sporozoites in the blood and liver (BL) following intravenous (i.v.) parasite inoculation which bypasses the skin (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Potocnjak et al., 1980; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Potocnjak et al., 1980; Wang et al., 2020

claim: Antibody cytotoxicity is thought to be responsible for sporozoite neutralization in the liver.
source: Ab cytotoxicity is also thought to be responsible for sporozoite neutralization in the liver (Wang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020

claim: Some highly cytotoxic antibodies were not able to significantly decrease infection following an intravenous sporozoite inoculation.
source: Ab cytotoxicity is also thought to be responsible for sporozoite neutralization in the liver (Wang et al., 2020), but some highly cytotoxic Abs were not able to significantly decrease infection following an i.v. sporozoite inoculation (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023

claim: 3D11 is a cytotoxic monoclonal antibody against the CSP of Plasmodium berghei.
source: In this study, we analyzed how 3D11, a cytotoxic mAb against the CSP of Plasmodium berghei (Pb)
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript

claim: 3D11 inhibits parasite motility and kills sporozoites in vitro.
source: In this study, we analyzed how 3D11, a cytotoxic mAb against the CSP of Plasmodium berghei (Pb) which has been shown to inhibit parasite motility and kill sporozoites in vitro (Aliprandini et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Aliprandini et al., 2018

claim: 3D11 inhibits sporozoite motility in the skin.
source: In this study, we analyzed how 3D11, a cytotoxic mAb against the CSP of Plasmodium berghei (Pb) which has been shown to inhibit parasite motility and kill sporozoites in vitro (Aliprandini et al., 2018), as well as to inhibit motility in the skin (Flores-Garcia et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Flores-Garcia et al., 2018

claim: Passive transfer of 100 µg of mAb 3D11 sterilely protected animals when sporozoites were inoculated in the skin by micro-injection (100%).
source: Passive transfer of 100 µg of mAb 3D11 sterilely protected animals only when sporozoites were inoculated in the skin, either by micro-injection (100%) or by mosquito bite (86%, Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B

claim: Passive transfer of 100 µg of mAb 3D11 sterilely protected 86% of animals when sporozoites were inoculated by mosquito bite.
source: Passive transfer of 100 µg of mAb 3D11 sterilely protected animals only when sporozoites were inoculated in the skin, either by micro-injection (100%) or by mosquito bite (86%, Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B

claim: 3D11 led to a tenfold reduction in parasitemia after intravenous challenge.
source: Despite not eliciting sterile protection, 3D11 led to a tenfold reduction in parasitemia after i.v. challenge (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: 3D11 led to a delayed prepatency in passively immunized mice compared to the control group after intravenous challenge.
source: Despite not eliciting sterile protection, 3D11 led to a tenfold reduction in parasitemia after i.v. challenge (Figure 1A), and accordingly, a delayed prepatency in passively immunized mice compared to the control group (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The bite challenge is more comparable to the skin challenge than the intravenous challenge.
source: These results confirm that the bite challenge is more comparable to the skin challenge than the i.v. challenge, as previously observed (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023 and Aliprandini et al., 2018

claim: 3D11 predominantly neutralizes sporozoites in the skin, but also targets sporozoites in the blood and liver.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that 3D11 predominantly neutralizes sporozoites in the skin, but also targets sporozoites in the BL (Flores-Garcia et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Flores-Garcia et al., 2018

claim: Increasing the mAb dose to 300 µg further reduced the parasitemia by ~100-fold compared to the control.
source: Increasing the mAb dose to 300 µg further reduced the parasitemia by ~100-fold compared to the control (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: A threefold increase of the mAb dose (from 100 to 300 µg) failed to confer sterile protection against intravenous challenge.
source: However, this threefold increase of the mAb dose still failed to confer sterile protection against i.v. challenge while 100 µg of 3D11 were sufficient to clear the infection in 86–100% of the mice after skin or bite challenge (Figure 1A, C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, C

claim: 3D11 sporozoite neutralization in the blood and liver is concentration dependent but is not as efficient as in the skin.
source: These results indicate that 3D11 sporozoite neutralization in the BL is concentration dependent but is not as efficient as in the skin.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data comparing different doses and routes of challenge

claim: 3D11 neither significantly killed parasites at 7 minutes post-inoculation nor affected sporozoite arrest in the liver.
source: The total flux and the percentage of signal in the liver were not affected by the presence of 3D11 (83% for control vs. 87% for 3D11-treated mice p = 0.36, Figure 2C, D, 7 min), indicating that 3D11 neither significantly killed parasites at this early time point of infection nor affected sporozoite arrest in the liver.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 2C, D

claim: Most sporozoites cross the liver sinusoidal barrier within 3 hr post-intravenous inoculation.
source: Since most sporozoites cross the liver sinusoidal barrier within 3 hr post-i.v. inoculation (Mathieu et al., 2015; Tavares et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mathieu et al., 2015 and Tavares et al., 2013

claim: At 4 hr post-inoculation, the difference in parasite load between the 3D11- and the vehicle-treated group was approximately twofold, but it was not statistically different.
source: At 4 hr, the difference between the 3D11- and the vehicle-treated group was ~twofold, but it was not statistically different.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data

claim: At 24 hr post-inoculation, a >20-fold decrease in the relative parasite load was evident in 3D11-treated mice compared to controls (p = 0.008).
source: In comparison, at 24 hr, a >20-fold decrease in the relative parasite load was evident (p = 0.008, Figure 2D, E).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 2D, E

claim: 3D11 requires more than 4 hr to eliminate most parasites in the liver.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that 3D11, rather than having an early effect on i.v. inoculated sporozoites in the blood circulation for example, by inhibiting the homing or killing the parasite in the blood, requires more than 4 hr to eliminate most parasites in the liver.
evidence: Inferred from bioluminescence data showing temporal progression of parasite elimination

claim: 3D11 did not impair parasite arrest in the liver sinusoids or significantly kill sporozoites during the first 2 hr after intravenous inoculation.
source: Equivalent numbers of susceptible (n = 80) and non-susceptible (n = 86) sporozoites were observed by microscopy in the analyzed fields, indicating that 3D11 did not impair parasite arrest in the liver sinusoids or significantly kill sporozoites during the first 2 hr after i.v. inoculation (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Already 10 min after inoculation, 3D11-susceptible parasites displayed a strong impairment in motility compared to the control parasites in passively immunized mice.
source: Already 10 min after inoculation, 3D11-susceptible parasites displayed a strong impairment in motility compared to the control parasites in passively immunized mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Thirty minutes after sporozoite injection, almost none of the susceptible Pb mCherry parasites were motile while 50% of the control PbPf GFP sporozoites were still moving.
source: Thirty minutes after sporozoite injection, almost none of the susceptible Pb mCherry parasites were motile while 50% of the control PbPf GFP sporozoites were still moving.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data

claim: Only 52% of the Pb mCherry susceptible sporozoites were found in the parenchyma in contrast to 89% of non-susceptible parasites, indicating that 3D11 affects sporozoite entry into the hepatic parenchyma.
source: Strikingly, only 52% of the Pb mCherry susceptible sporozoites were found in the parenchyma in contrast to 89% of non-susceptible parasites, indicating that 3D11 affects sporozoite entry into the hepatic parenchyma (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Ex vivo, after 1 hr, 97% of the control parasites were inside the parenchyma in contrast to 53% of the susceptible sporozoites.
source: Ex vivo, we observed that after 1 hr, 97% of the control parasites (n = 34) were inside the parenchyma in contrast to 53% of the susceptible sporozoites (n = 45), confirming the results of the in vivo experiments.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo microscopy data

claim: 3D11 blocks sporozoite entry into the hepatic parenchyma by around twofold.
source: Since comparable numbers of Pb mCherry and PbPf GFP sporozoites were found in the microscopic fields quantified in vivo and ex vivo (Figure 3D), we can infer that 3D11 blocks sporozoite entry into the hepatic parenchyma by around twofold.
evidence: Inferred from microscopy data shown in Figure 3D

claim: In 3D11-treated mice, most sporozoites die in the hepatic parenchyma probably due to the loss of fitness caused by the 3D11 mAb.
source: Hence, in 3D11-treated mice, most sporozoites die in the hepatic parenchyma probably due to the loss of fitness caused by the 3D11 mAb.
evidence: Inferred from the discrepancy between the twofold reduction in parenchyma entry and the larger reduction in parasitemia

claim: Increasing concentrations of 3D11 were associated with a drastic reduction in the number of recovered extracellular sporozoites.
source: At 2 hr, increasing concentrations of 3D11 were associated with a drastic reduction in the number of recovered extracellular sporozoites as well as a marked decrease in the percentage of GFP+ invaded cells compared to PBS controls.
evidence: Supported by in vitro invasion assay data

claim: Increasing concentrations of 3D11 were associated with a marked decrease in the percentage of GFP+ invaded cells compared to PBS controls.
source: At 2 hr, increasing concentrations of 3D11 were associated with a drastic reduction in the number of recovered extracellular sporozoites as well as a marked decrease in the percentage of GFP+ invaded cells compared to PBS controls.
evidence: Supported by in vitro invasion assay data

claim: 3D11 kills and inhibits parasite entry into cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: 3D11, therefore, kills and inhibits parasite entry into cells in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4B, 2 hr).
evidence: Supported by in vitro invasion assay data shown in Figure 4B

claim: There is a dose-dependent decrease in the number of intracellularly developing parasites when comparing the recently invaded cells (2 hr) with later time points (15 and 44 hr).
source: Interestingly, we observed a dose-dependent decrease in the number of intracellularly developing parasites when comparing the recently invaded cells (2 hr) with later time points (Figure 4C, 2 hr vs. 15 and 44 hr).
evidence: Supported by in vitro development assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The exposition of sporozoites for 2 hr with 5 µg/ml of 3D11 led to a more than 50% reduction in the post-invasion number of intracellular parasites at 15 and 44 hr.
source: For example, the exposition of sporozoites for 2 hr with 5 µg/ml of 3D11 led to a more than 50% reduction in the post-invasion number of intracellular parasites at 15 and 44 hr (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro development assay data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The dose-dependent loss of fitness caused by 3D11 mAb was demonstrated by decreasing GFP intensities of the surviving EEFs.
source: The dose-dependent loss of fitness caused by 3D11 mAb was also demonstrated by decreasing GFP intensities of the surviving EEFs (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Post-invasion labeling of 3D11 bound to the membrane of intracellular parasites revealed a strong staining surrounding the parasite at 2 and 15 hr, but only punctual traces of 3D11 at 44 hr.
source: Post-invasion labeling of 3D11 bound to the membrane of intracellular parasites revealed a strong staining surrounding the parasite at 2 and 15 hr, but only punctual traces of 3D11 at 44 hr (Figure 4F, 3D11 - cyan).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F

claim: CSP was detected surrounding the control parasites at all time points (2, 15, and 44 hr).
source: Of note, CSP was detected surrounding the control parasites at all time points indicating that the lack of staining at 44 hr is not due to a decrease in the CSP amount on the parasite surface (Figure 4F, CSP, Control).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F

claim: 3D11 incubated from 2 to 44 hr with invaded cells had no effect on the parasite intracellular development.
source: To evaluate the potential post-invasion entry of 3D11 into the PV of infected cells and posterior neutralization of intracellular parasites, we incubated invaded cells from 2 to 44 hr with 3D11, but no effect on the parasite intracellular development was observed (Figure 4G, 2 hr p.i.).
evidence: Supported by in vitro development assay data shown in Figure 4G

claim: The late inhibition of parasite development is already achieved at 15 hr and likely caused by antibodies dragged inside cells bound to sporozoites before or during the invasion.
source: Altogether, our results indicate that the late inhibition of parasite development is already achieved at 15 hr and likely caused by Abs dragged inside cells bound to sporozoites before or during the invasion.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro development assay data and immunofluorescence observations

claim: 3D11 not only inhibits sporozoite entry into host cells but also affects its fitness resulting in subsequent parasite killing hours after invasion.
source: In line with the late sporozoite neutralization effect observed in the liver, the in vitro assay demonstrates that 3D11 not only inhibits sporozoite entry into host cells but also affects its fitness resulting in subsequent parasite killing hours after invasion.
evidence: Supported by in vitro invasion and development assay data

claim: In the control group at 2 hr, the UIS4-negative population represented 14% of intracellular parasites, while in the 3D11-treated group, it reached 48%.
source: However, while at 2 hr in the control group, this population represented 14% of intracellular parasites, in the 3D11-treated group, it reached 48% (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The ~threefold increase in the UIS4-negative population could explain the late killing of intracellular sporozoites by 3D11.
source: This ~threefold increase in the UIS4-negative population could explain the late killing of intracellular sporozoites by 3D11.
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence data showing increased UIS4-negative parasites

claim: At 44 hr, surviving EEFs in the 3D11-treated samples presented a similar area and UIS4 staining intensity than control parasites.
source: At 44 hr, surviving EEFs in the 3D11-treated samples presented a similar area and UIS4 staining intensity than control parasites (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C, D

claim: The GFP intensity of 3D11-treated parasites at 44 hr was significantly lower than control EEFs.
source: However, as observed by flow cytometry (Figure 4D), the GFP intensity of 3D11-treated parasites was significantly lower than control EEFs, indicating that 3D11 can somehow affect protein expression with undetermined effects in the genesis of red blood cell infecting stages.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and flow cytometry data in Figure 4D

claim: The skin plays a major role in parasite-dependent cytotoxicity induced by anti-CSP antibodies.
source: The skin plays a major role in parasite-dependent cytotoxicity induced by anti-CSP Abs (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018; Flores-Garcia et al., 2018; Vanderberg and Frevert, 2004).

claim: In the skin, monoclonal antibodies inhibit sporozoite motility and induce CSP shedding, leading to loss of their infectivity and death.
source: In the skin, mAbs inhibit sporozoite motility (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018; Flores-Garcia et al., 2018; Vanderberg and Frevert, 2004) and induce CSP shedding, leading to loss of their infectivity and death (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Potent monoclonal antibodies can provide protection when parasites are introduced directly into the bloodstream.

evidence: Supported by citation to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023

claim: The extra-cutaneous neutralizing activity is a characteristic of the most potent protective antibodies.

evidence: Supported by citation to Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023

claim: The killing of skin escapees is critical for sterilizing immunity.
source: Despite having lower protective efficiency in the BL than in the skin, this extra-cutaneous neutralizing activity is a characteristic of the most potent protective Abs (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023), indicating that the killing of skin escapees is critical for sterilizing immunity.

claim: In the hepatic environment, cytotoxic antibodies have been shown to prevent parasite egress from sinusoids, hinder cell traversal, and kill sporozoites.

claim: The hepatic cytotoxic neutralizing activities of different antibodies do not always match their protective activity.
source: However, the hepatic cytotoxic neutralizing activities of these different Abs do not always match their protective activity.

claim: 3D11 is less effective in the bloodstream than in the skin.

claim: High amounts of 3D11 transferred to mice are required to provide sterile protection after an intravenous challenge.

claim: The repeat region of Pb CSP is not involved in the sporozoite homing to the liver.

claim: The bioluminescent signal in 3D11-treated mice only decreases ~30% at 4 hr post-sporozoite inoculation indicating that most parasites are lately killed by 3D11.

claim: 3D11 inhibits sporozoite motility and limits their exit from the liver sinusoids.
source: These results suggest that 3D11 inhibits sporozoite motility and limits their exit from the liver sinusoids, as previously reported (Wang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data and citation to Wang et al., 2020

claim: The twofold difference in parasite translocation alone cannot completely explain the ~100-fold reduction of parasitemia observed 3 days later in 3D11-treated versus control groups.
source: but this twofold difference in parasite translocation alone cannot completely explain the ~100-fold reduction of parasitemia observed 3 days later in 3D11-treated versus control groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of microscopy and parasitemia data

claim: 3D11-susceptible parasites rarely fragmented and died in vivo during 3 hr of continuous imaging.
source: During 3 hr of continuous imaging, it was observed that 3D11-susceptible parasites rarely fragmented and died in vivo.

claim: Potent PfCSP human monoclonal antibodies caused 20 and 40% of sporozoites to die while recording their in vivo effect in the liver.

claim: The cytotoxicity of anti-CSP antibodies correlates with sporozoite loss of fitness.
source: It is important to note that the cytotoxicity of anti-CSP Abs correlates with sporozoite loss of fitness (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023), quantified by the inhibition of motility, the loss of infectivity, and the killing of sporozoites (Aguirre-Botero et al., 2023; Aliprandini et al., 2018).
